author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Restore broken bloom in hardware rendering without overexposing the scene
summary: Use paired bright and dark checkpoints to identify a missing or misaligned framebuffer pass, compare a software reference, and find the least expensive blending or native-scaling correction.
heroAlt: God of War PCSX2 capture showing an incorrectly rendered bright bloom and fog pass

sourceLabels.pcsx2-2-release: PCSX2 description of blending, framebuffer reads, and native scaling for bloom
sourceLabels.pcsx2-july-august-2015: PCSX2 before-and-after bloom and fog accuracy examples

blocks.text: Classify the bloom as absent, displaced, clipped, or excessive

Bloom is usually assembled from more than one pass: the game isolates bright information, filters or downsamples it, and composites the result over the scene. A hardware renderer can therefore fail in several visibly different ways. Missing bloom leaves light sources hard-edged; displaced bloom produces a ghost offset from the source; clipped bloom becomes a rectangle; excessive bloom washes out nearby geometry. Select one checkpoint with a strong isolated lamp or spell and another with small highlights against a dark background. Record the game's serial, internal resolution, renderer, GPU driver, blending accuracy, native-scaling status, and whether manual framebuffer or skip-draw fixes are active.
Do not evaluate bloom from a single overexposed phone photograph. Auto-exposure and HDR tone mapping can erase detail that is present in the emulator's actual frame.
Prepare two bloom scenes with luminance references

items: An in-game save before a repeatable bright effect with visible geometry immediately around it.
A second dark scene containing small emissive details, so a setting cannot pass merely by dimming the entire output.
Direct screenshots from native hardware output and a brief software-rendered correctness reference.
Post shaders, reshade layers, display HDR conversion, texture replacement, and custom color controls disabled.
A warm-session performance sample from the bright scene and a backup of the title's graphics profile.

blocks.text: Separate composition accuracy from upscale alignment

items: 1. Cold-start the bright checkpoint at native internal resolution with automatic blending and capture the source plus surrounding detail.
2. Render the same moment briefly in software mode and compare bloom radius, center, occlusion, and whether foreground objects correctly block the glow.
3. Return to hardware mode and compare supported graphics APIs without altering the driver or resolution; retain the path that most closely preserves the reference.
4. When bloom is missing or clips into a solid shape at native resolution, raise blending accuracy one tier, restart the scene, and stop at the first tier that restores composition.
5. When native hardware is correct but bloom separates from its light only after upscaling, restore automatic blending and test the emulator's documented native-scaling correction instead.
6. Replay the dark checkpoint and confirm that small highlights glow without lifting black backgrounds or whitening character textures.
7. Warm the device, measure the effects-heavy sequence, and compare barrier, render-pass, or readback counters if the build exposes them.
8. Save only the successful branch in this game's profile and annotate whether it addresses blending at native output or post-process alignment while upscaled.

blocks.text: Blending accuracy governs how faithfully hardware rendering reproduces interactions with previous framebuffer contents, while native scaling targets post-process passes that were authored to operate at the PS2's original scale. They solve related-looking symptoms at different stages. Software rendering supplies a composition reference because it can reproduce GS behavior more directly, but its speed is not the acceptance target. The two-scene test prevents a false fix where reducing brightness makes one blown-out lamp appear better while deleting intended glow elsewhere.
The selected profile must preserve the effect's shape, depth relationship, tonal range, and playability.

items: The glow is centered on the emitting object and follows it during camera or character movement.
Foreground geometry occludes bloom where the software reference shows an obstruction.
Bright surfaces retain texture detail instead of collapsing into a uniform white patch.
The dark checkpoint preserves black areas and still displays its small intended highlights.
Sustained frame pacing remains acceptable after thermal stabilization and no unrelated transparency regresses.

blocks.text: Bloom results that require another investigation

items: Software output has the same abnormal glow: confirm the scene reference and remove game patches or texture modifications.
Only the physical display blooms while direct screenshots are balanced: audit HDR, color range, panel enhancement, and camera exposure.
A higher blending tier fixes the lamp but corrupts shadows or fog: revert it and collect a title-specific rendering report.
The effect drifts only at one unusual custom resolution: use a supported integer multiplier before adding any manual offset.

blocks.text: Set blending to Automatic, disable the tested native-scaling or offset override, restore the original API, and restart the application. Replay both checkpoints to confirm the previous symptom is reproducible; then choose the last lower tier that passed performance or return to native resolution until a precise correction exists.
Intentional glare can be visually aggressive

Some PS2 games deliberately use broad, bright bloom. The goal is fidelity to a trustworthy reference, not uniformly subdued lighting. Avoid publishing a global recommendation from one title, because framebuffer formats, blend equations, and post-process scaling differ between engines and even between scenes.
